channel.title: horowitz.law: Georgia Appellate Watch
channel.description: AI-assisted synopses of new Georgia appellate, Eleventh Circuit, and U.S. Supreme Court opinions, filtered for civil litigation and insurance practice. Each synopsis is AI-drafted; the linked opinion is the authority. A curated core, not a complete docket. This feed covers the most recent two years; older opinions are archived by year at https://horowitz.law/archive.

item.title: Robertson v. Toyota Motor Corporation (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: A tenant died in his sleep of carbon monoxide poisoning after leaving his keyless-ignition vehicle running in the attached garage below his apartment, and his estate sued the out-of-possession landlord for failing to install a carbon monoxide detector. The Court of Appeals affirmed summary judgment for the landlord, holding that O.C.G.A. section 44-7-14 imposes only a duty arising from defective construction or a failure to keep the premises in repair and does not create a duty of maintenance, and that the absence of a detector from the outset did not show the apartment had deteriorated from its original condition so as to require repair. The court also rejected the estate's implied-warranty-of-habitability theory drawn from Thompson v. Crownover, noting that the duties imposed by O.C.G.A. section 44-7-13 sound in contract rather than tort and that any expansion of an out-of-possession landlord's duty must come from the legislature. It further held that arguments about the condition of the premises before the tenant took possession were not preserved. Why it matters: The decision reinforces that an out-of-possession landlord's tort exposure under O.C.G.A. section 44-7-14 is confined to defective construction and failure to repair, and that a claim framed as a failure to maintain or as a breach of an implied warranty of habitability does not state a tort claim against such a landlord. Also: The court affirmed the exclusion of the estate's automotive mechanical engineering expert, who would have opined that the keyless ignition system was defective for lacking an automatic shut-off and that such a feature was technically and economically feasible. Applying O.C.G.A. section 24-7-702(b) and Daubert, the court found no abuse of discretion where the expert did not examine the subject vehicle or an exemplar of the same model year, could not access certain vehicle data, performed no testing or benchmarking, and where the proponent identified no methodology reliably applied to the facts of the case. The court also held that a trial court is not required to make detailed findings when ruling on a motion to exclude expert testimony, because neither O.C.G.A. section 24-7-702 nor case law imposes that requirement. Why it matters: The ruling illustrates that reliance on general experience with similar fact patterns, without case-specific facts, data, or an articulated and applied methodology, can support exclusion under Rule 702(b), and confirms that trial courts need not enter detailed findings on such motions. Also: The court affirmed the admission of the estate's human factors expert, who opined on the adequacy of the vehicle's warning system, the applicable standard of care, and a risk ranking derived from a National Safety Council system. It held that the manufacturer failed to explain why the expert's own human-subject testing was necessary where the expert relied on the manufacturer's own human-subject studies, industry standards and guidelines, decibel testing of the warning beeps against ambient engine noise, and other indicia of reliability. The court further held that publication on the specific topic is a relevant but not dispositive consideration and is not a prerequisite to admissibility, and that a party's mere invitation to the trial court to apply an outdated pre-2013 standard is not itself trial court error. Why it matters: The decision applies the flexible reliability inquiry to a human-factors warnings expert, confirming that a party challenging an expert must explain why particular testing or publication was necessary to reliability rather than simply noting its absence. Also: The court reversed the denial of the manufacturer's motion for partial summary judgment on punitive damages, holding that punitive damages are not available in a Georgia wrongful death action because allowing both the full value of the life and punitive damages would impose a double penalty. After the estate withdrew its pain and suffering claim, it could not attach punitive damages to remaining claims for funeral and ante mortem expenses, because those expenses grew out of the wrongful death and O.C.G.A. section 51-4-5 operates as a true wrongful death provision rather than a mere survival statute. The court noted that it lacks authority to overturn the controlling Supreme Court precedent the estate asked it to reject. Why it matters: The holding confirms that punitive damages remain categorically unavailable in a wrongful death action and that pecuniary claims for funeral and ante mortem expenses arising from the death cannot serve as a predicate for them. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10963742/toyota-motor-corporation-v-james-louis-robertson/

item.title: Jane Doe v. Carnival Corporation (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: A cruise passenger sued the cruise line on general maritime law theories arising from an encounter with a crewmember; the district court granted the passenger partial summary judgment on false imprisonment liability after excluding FBI reports in their entirety as hearsay, and a jury later found the cruise line liable for sexual assault and awarded about $10.25 million. The Eleventh Circuit held that the district court erred by treating the reports as a single hearsay unit: while the crewmember's embedded statements were inadmissible double hearsay, the investigating agent's own conclusions required their own analysis under Federal Rule of Evidence 803(8), and the opponent of admission bears the burden of showing a lack of trustworthiness under the timeliness, skill and experience, hearing, and bias factors. The court found that burden unmet, held the agent's consensual-encounter conclusion was not barred by Rule 403 at the summary judgment stage (while noting the fact of a declination to prosecute is likely unduly prejudicial), and noted that hearsay may be considered on summary judgment if it can be reduced to admissible form, such as by live testimony. Because that conclusion created a genuine dispute on consent, partial summary judgment was reversed. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that an investigator's own factual findings in a government report receive an independent Federal Rule of Evidence 803(8) analysis separate from third-party statements quoted within the report, and that the party opposing admission carries the burden of showing untrustworthiness. Also: Addressing its own jurisdiction, the court explained that a partial summary judgment order resolving liability but leaving damages and other claims for further proceedings is never final for purposes of 28 U.S.C. section 1291, so an immediate appeal would have been dismissed as premature. After trial and entry of final judgment, however, the interlocutory order merged into the final judgment and became reviewable. The court therefore reached the partial summary judgment ruling even though the appeal followed a jury verdict. Why it matters: It confirms both that a partial summary judgment on liability cannot be appealed when entered and that the ruling remains reviewable after final judgment through merger. Also: The court then considered the effect of the erroneous partial summary judgment on the trial and found it could have affected the outcome in three respects: the same hearsay analysis led to wholesale exclusion of the reports at trial, which barred the agent from testifying to her conclusions and barred cross-examination of the passenger's security and damages experts about the reports they had relied on; the jury was instructed that liability for false imprisonment was established and that the passenger was unlawfully restrained against her will, which could color its view of consent; and the finding of consent was relevant to both the false imprisonment and the sexual assault claims, which arose from the same events. The court vacated the judgment on those two claims and remanded for a new trial on them, while holding that the negligence and intentional infliction claims decided for the cruise line would not be relitigated because the passenger did not cross-appeal. Why it matters: The opinion illustrates that an erroneous pretrial liability ruling entangled with the evidence and jury instructions can require a new trial on related claims, and that the scope of the new trial is limited by the absence of a cross-appeal on claims resolved adversely to the appellee. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10957668/jane-doe-v-carnival-corporation/

item.title: Richardson v. Thunder, LLC (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Guests injured or killed in a multi-shooter shooting at an annual fraternity homecoming block party sued the national fraternity and the limited liability company that owned the house, asserting premises liability, negligence, and nuisance. Applying the Carmichael totality-of-the-circumstances framework, the Court of Appeals held that evidence of occasional fistfights at parties four or more years earlier and three police responses for crowd control or disorderly conduct, none involving weapons, injuries, or arrests, was not substantially similar to a multiparty shootout and did not create a jury issue on reasonable foreseeability. The court also found no other totality factors, such as a high-crime location, weapons previously observed at the parties, or a volatile situation brewing that night, and rejected the contention that a large party with alcohol is itself enough, noting that would make the proprietor an insurer of guest safety. Because no duty to guard against the criminal act arose, summary judgment was proper for both the fraternity and the property owner, and the derivative vicarious-liability claim failed for want of an underlying tort; the court noted the 2025 negligent security statutes, O.C.G.A. sections 51-3-50 through 51-3-57, do not apply to causes of action arising before April 21, 2025. Affirmed. Why it matters: The decision applies the Carmichael foreseeability analysis to hold that generalized prior fights and crowd-control police calls are not substantially similar to a mass shooting, and confirms that the invitee/licensee distinction is largely irrelevant to third-party criminal conduct claims while the 2025 negligent security statutes do not reach earlier-arising claims. Also: The court separately affirmed summary judgment on claims that the national fraternity negligently failed to supervise and monitor its undergraduate chapter so as to prevent hazardous conditions on the property. It held that negligent supervision or monitoring imposes liability only where it is reasonably foreseeable that the supervised party could cause the type of harm sustained, and that an independent intervening criminal act of a third party is treated as the proximate cause. Given the absence of evidence of foreseeability, the random shooting of partygoers was not a reasonably foreseeable result of any supervisory failure. Why it matters: It confirms that a negligent supervision or monitoring theory against a parent organization rises or falls on the same foreseeability and proximate-cause analysis that governs the underlying premises claim for third-party criminal conduct. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10956632/tamia-richardson-v-thunder-llc/

item.title: Fulton v. Fayette Community Hospital, Inc. (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: A pro se plaintiff sued a hospital and providers over emergency-room care following a motor vehicle collision, supporting her claims with affidavits from a primary care physician. The trial court found the affiant unqualified under OCGA 24-7-702(c)(2), which supplies the competency standard for affidavits required by OCGA 9-11-9.1, because he had not shown regular active practice in emergency medicine for at least three of the five years preceding the alleged malpractice. The Court of Appeals reviewed for abuse of discretion, noting the affiant's curriculum vitae showed only primary care and personal injury practice plus continuing medical education, and affirmed the competency ruling. Why it matters: The decision reiterates that adding a specialty to an expert affidavit's list of areas of expertise does not satisfy OCGA 24-7-702(c)(2) without a showing of regular active practice in that specialty during the statutory period. Also: The court held that the trial court erred in treating every count as sounding in professional negligence. Claims for fraud and misrepresentation about a physician assistant's licensure, negligence per se based on statutes and rules barring unlicensed persons from holding themselves out as physicians, willful destruction or falsification of medical records, intentional infliction of emotional distress based on intentional conduct, breach of fiduciary duty premised on falsification and concealment, ordinary negligence in administrative acts by the hospital, negligent hiring, retention, and supervision as to intentional conduct, and the derivative punitive damages count do not require an expert affidavit, and their dismissal was reversed. The court affirmed dismissal of the withdrawn-consent battery count, because whether it was medically feasible to stop treatment requires professional judgment, of the race discrimination count, because it rested on a failure to meet the standard of care, and of the catch-all negligence and gross negligence count, because it challenged the adequacy of medical treatment and the discharge decision. Why it matters: The opinion draws a count-by-count line between allegations of intentional or administrative conduct that fall outside OCGA 9-11-9.1 and allegations that implicate professional skill and judgment and therefore require a compliant expert affidavit. Also: The plaintiff argued the trial court lost jurisdiction to dismiss because a notice of appeal from the denial of her summary judgment motion was pending. The court held that supersedeas under OCGA 5-6-46(a) attaches only upon payment of costs, and nothing showed the plaintiff paid the cost bill. Independently, because an order denying summary judgment is reviewable only through the interlocutory procedures of OCGA 5-6-34(b), a notice of appeal filed without a certificate of immediate review and appellate grant is ineffective as supersedeas even if costs are paid, so the trial court retained jurisdiction. Why it matters: It confirms that a premature notice of appeal from an order denying summary judgment does not divest the trial court of jurisdiction, both for failure to pay costs and for failure to follow interlocutory appeal procedures. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10954168/erika-fulton-v-fayette-community-hospital-inc/

item.title: Jackson v. Cantrell (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Plaintiff was shot accidentally by a 15-year-old passenger inside a truck owned by the teen's father, and after suit he signed a limited release under OCGA 33-24-41.1 that released the settling insurer and the individual defendants except to the extent other insurance coverage is available covering his claims. Applying Harvey v. Hall, the court held that a defendant moving for summary judgment on the release as an affirmative defense bears the initial burden of establishing the prima facie defense, including that no other coverage applies, before the burden shifts to the plaintiff. The court noted that affirmative evidence of coverage denial is unnecessary for a policy plainly inapplicable on its face, but here the movants did not address the commercial auto policy's non-owned auto provision covering vehicles owned by LLC members used in the business or personal affairs, or its permissive-user definition of insured, so they failed to carry that initial burden. The court expressly did not decide whether coverage actually exists, and reversed the grant of summary judgment. Why it matters: It clarifies how the burden-shifting framework for a limited-release affirmative defense operates when other policies exist, requiring the movant to account for the policy's own coverage-granting provisions rather than relying on scheduled vehicles and drivers alone. Also: The defendants argued the appeal should be affirmed because the appellant did not designate the entire record for transmission. The court rejected that contention, holding that because it may consider the record from a prior appeal in the same case, an appellant need not designate for inclusion parts of the record already before the court from that earlier appeal. The court also observed that nothing necessary for review was missing. Why it matters: It confirms that a notice of appeal limited to materials filed since a prior appeal in the same case is not a fatal record defect. Also: The appellant contended the trial court erred by ignoring an amended complaint seeking a declaratory judgment that the LLC's commercial auto policy provided coverage. The court declined to address the amended complaint's propriety in the first instance because it sits to correct errors of law made by trial courts. It further noted that its prior affirmance of summary judgment for the LLC is the law of the case and binding in subsequent proceedings, so the LLC is no longer a party. Why it matters: It reiterates that an appellate court will not rule on a matter the trial court never addressed and that an earlier affirmance of summary judgment for a party removes that party from the case as law of the case. Also: The trial court had awarded attorney fees to defense counsel under OCGA 9-11-68 based on its grant of summary judgment. Because that award depended on the summary judgment ruling the court reversed, the court also reversed the fee award. Why it matters: It confirms that an OCGA 9-11-68 fee award falls with the underlying judgment that supported it. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10953750/bryson-jackson-v-parker-cantrell/

item.title: Clark v. Northeast Georgia Medical Center, Inc. (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Plaintiff alleged that an unidentified hospital employee dropped her husband while transferring him from one bed to another, causing injuries that led to his death, and pleaded ordinary negligence without the expert affidavit required by OCGA 9-11-9.1. The trial court dismissed, finding that transferring a patient is an exercise of expert medical judgment. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that, construing the complaint favorably to plaintiff, the alleged drop does not necessarily implicate a medical question and may instead be a physical act of strength and dexterity, and noting that the record did not establish that the unidentified employee was among the professionals covered by OCGA 9-11-9.1 (g). Why it matters: It clarifies that a patient fall during a physical transfer is not automatically a professional negligence claim requiring an expert affidavit, and that a defendant's status as a covered professional matters at the pleading stage. Also: The trial court also held that plaintiff could not cure the affidavit defect by an amended complaint filed after the two-year medical malpractice limitation period expired. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that because the original complaint stated a claim for ordinary negligence, plaintiff was authorized under OCGA 9-11-15 (a) to amend as a matter of course to add an alternative professional negligence count with a supporting expert affidavit. Because the added claim arose from the same occurrence, it related back to the timely original complaint under OCGA 9-11-15 (c) and was not time barred. Why it matters: It confirms that an alternative professional negligence count with an expert affidavit, added after the limitation period, relates back to a timely complaint that stated an ordinary negligence claim arising from the same occurrence. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10953294/brenda-clark-v-northeast-georgia-medical-center-inc/

item.title: Travelers Property Casualty Insurance Company v. Kamesha Davis (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: An insurer sought a declaration that the policyholder's adult daughter, injured in a collision while staying at one of the policyholder's houses, was not a "resident relative" entitled to uninsured motorist coverage. Applying Georgia law, the Eleventh Circuit affirmed the conclusion that the daughter was a resident of that house rather than a transient visitor, because she was living there exclusively at the relevant time and Georgia law requires only an intent to live in a place "for the time being," not permanently; her earlier plans to relocate to another state did not defeat residency. The court treated residence and household membership as separate requirements under the policy definition. Why it matters: The decision separates the residency inquiry from the household inquiry in Georgia "resident relative" UM disputes and confirms that unrealized plans to move elsewhere do not by themselves negate residence at the place where a claimant is actually living. Also: On the second requirement, whether the claimant was a resident of the policyholder's household, the court reversed summary judgment for the claimant and found a genuine dispute of material fact. A jury could find that the policyholder maintained her household at the address where she ran an assisted living facility and slept most nights rather than at the house where the daughter lived, and, even assuming the household was at that house, the conflicting deposition testimony about utilities, phone bills, groceries, cooking, and reimbursement did not compel a finding that mother and daughter had merged households rather than maintaining separate households under different managements. The court noted that Georgia's appellate courts have not decided whether a person may maintain more than one household, and that evidence about family living arrangements generally is not susceptible to summary adjudication. Why it matters: It clarifies that household membership is a distinct, fact-intensive element of "resident relative" coverage that turns on the aggregate details of the living arrangement and financial interdependence, and that mixed evidence on those points ordinarily precludes summary judgment for either side. Also: Raising the issue on its own, the court confirmed diversity jurisdiction by measuring the amount in controversy in a declaratory coverage action from the insurer's perspective as the value of the object of the litigation. Because the claimant had made a pre-suit demand exceeding $75,000 and the policy's $100,000 uninsured motorist limit would theoretically permit recovery of that amount, the insurer carried its burden of proving the jurisdictional minimum by a preponderance of the evidence. Why it matters: It illustrates how the amount in controversy is measured in an insurer-filed declaratory judgment action, using the pre-suit demand together with the applicable policy limit. Unpublished; not binding precedent. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10953092/travelers-property-casualty-insurance-company-v-kamesha-davis/

item.title: Estancia US Limited Partnership v. Aji-Dawkins (Fla. DCA)
item.category: District Court of Appeal of Florida
item.description: In a premises case arising from a fall when a PVC railing gave way at a hotel's second-story walkway, the trial court granted plaintiff leave to amend to add a punitive damages claim based on gross negligence. Applying the Florida Supreme Court's recent clarification of the section 768.72(1) evidentiary-sufficiency test, the Sixth DCA reviewed de novo, viewed the proffered record in the light most favorable to the claimant, and asked whether a reasonable person could conclude the defendant engaged in gross negligence as defined in section 768.72(2), together with the employer criteria of section 768.72(3). The court held the deposition testimony did not support the two pleaded bases, because the maintenance employee who described the railing as a breakaway product testified he did not tell the owner it was unsuitable until after the fall and never said he reported an earlier child-related railing failure to the owner, while the other employee testified no safety concerns were raised. The order permitting the amendment was reversed with instructions to vacate it, and the court separately directed that a copy of the opinion be sent to The Florida Bar based on trial counsel's misrepresentations of the deposition record at the hearing and in the proposed written order. Why it matters: The decision applies the clarified section 768.72(1) standard for pleading punitive damages, confirming that the reviewing court does not weigh evidence but tests whether the proffered record itself, read favorably to the claimant, could support a finding of gross negligence under the statutory definitions and the employer-liability criteria. item.title: Citizens Property Insurance Corporation v. Nekouee (Fla. DCA)
item.category: District Court of Appeal of Florida
item.description: An insured demanded appraisal under his residential property policy, the appraisers agreed on the amount of loss, and the insured then refused to sign the insurer's appraisal award form and filed a declaratory judgment action seeking only a declaration about the form's enforceability and his rights under the policy, without seeking damages. The trial court denied the insurer's motion to dismiss for failure to give the presuit notice required by section 627.70152(3)(a), Florida Statutes. The Second District held that section 627.70152(1)'s application to "all suits arising under" a residential or commercial property insurance policy means all suits, including declaratory judgment actions that seek no monetary relief, and that the statutorily specified notice contents remain workable in that setting. The court found a departure from the essential requirements of law, granted certiorari, and quashed the order, noting that section 627.70152(5) directs dismissal without prejudice when the required notice was not given. Why it matters: The decision establishes that Florida's presuit notice condition precedent for property insurance suits reaches declaratory judgment actions seeking no damages, so claimants must serve the statutory notice before filing any such action and courts must dismiss without prejudice when it is absent. Also: The insured separately argued that his suit did not "arise under" the policy within the meaning of section 627.70152(1), relying on arbitration cases that read "arising out of" or "arising under" narrowly to reach only disputes relating to interpretation and performance of the contract. The court concluded that even under that narrower construction the suit arises under the policy, because the insured alleged a bona fide controversy over policy terms and resolving whether the appraisal award form imposed extracontractual conditions requires interpreting the policy. The court also rejected reliance on personal injury protection precedent construing a differently worded notice statute limited to actions "for benefits." Why it matters: The holding clarifies that a dispute over the form or terms used to conclude an appraisal is a suit "arising under" the property policy for presuit notice purposes because its resolution turns on policy interpretation. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10948474/citizens-property-insurance-corporation-v-nekouee/

item.title: Ex parte State Farm Fire and Casualty Company (In re Foor v. State Farm Fire and Casualty Company) (Ala.)
item.description: Homeowners suing their insurer for breach of contract and bad faith over a hail and wind roof claim obtained a protective order permitting their counsel to share materials designated confidential or trade secret with other bad-faith roof cases against the same insurer in which the same counsel appear, and to disclose such materials to governmental agencies with oversight authority. On the insurer's mandamus petition, the court held that Rule 26, Ala. R. Civ. P., does not categorically bar sharing provisions, reasoning that Rule 26(b)(1) governs what information may be obtained in discovery rather than what a party may do with it once obtained, and that absent a protective order parties may generally disseminate discovery materials. The court nevertheless concluded the trial court exceeded its discretion in the breadth of the sharing language and granted the petition in part, directing that the provision be narrowed with additional safeguards; it also clarified that whether particular materials are in fact confidential or trade secret was not before it, because the umbrella order postpones that question and places the burden on the insurer to justify a designation if challenged. Two justices dissented, arguing that sharing of trade-secret and confidential information is antithetical to Rule 26 absent a case-specific justification. Why it matters: The decision establishes that Alabama's discovery rules do not per se prohibit protective orders allowing discovery materials to be shared with counsel in parallel litigation, while confirming that trial courts must tailor such provisions, which shapes how confidentiality disputes over claims-handling materials are litigated. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10948454/in-re-james-m-foor-and-krystina-foor-v-state-farm-fire-and-casualty/

item.title: Lineberger v. Newberry (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: After prevailing in a quiet-title boundary dispute and having the judgment affirmed on appeal, the prevailing parties left a motion for attorney fees under OCGA section 9-15-14 pending for five years, taking no action until they filed a notice of hearing shortly before the five-year anniversary of the last written order. The trial court held the case stood automatically dismissed by operation of law under the five-year rule and that it therefore lacked jurisdiction over the fee motion. The Court of Appeals affirmed, holding that a pending OCGA section 9-15-14 motion is part of the original action rather than a separate case, so the case was not fully adjudicated and the exception excusing already-resolved cases from the five-year rule did not apply. Because no written order signed by the judge and filed with the clerk, including an order of continuance, was obtained within five years, the automatic dismissal took effect one day before the scheduled hearing. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that an unresolved attorney fee motion keeps a case pending for purposes of the five-year automatic dismissal rule under OCGA section 9-11-41(e), so parties with fee motions outstanding after judgment must obtain a written order or continuance within five years or lose the trial court's jurisdiction to decide the motion. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10947292/james-earl-lineberger-v-caryl-ellen-newberry/

item.title: Vainberg v. Florida Insurance Guaranty Association (Fla. DCA)
item.category: District Court of Appeal of Florida
item.description: Insureds whose water-damage claim the insurer elected to repair sued for breach of the resulting Drew repair contract, and after the insurer's insolvency the Florida Insurance Guaranty Association was substituted as defendant and a consent judgment for policy limits was entered. The Fourth District held that a suit for breach of a Drew repair contract falls within the fee-shifting scope of section 627.428, Florida Statutes (2015), because such a contract exists solely by virtue of the insurer's exercise of a repair right granted by the policy and the dispute therefore arises under the policy. The court also relied on the statute's disjunctive reference to a 'policy or contract executed by the insurer,' reasoning that an election-to-repair letter is itself a contract executed by the insurer and that reading 'contract' as adding nothing would render it superfluous. The order denying fees was reversed and the case remanded to determine the amount. Why it matters: The decision establishes that an insurer's election to repair does not remove a subsequent breach claim from the reach of section 627.428's one-way fee-shifting provision. Also: The court separately held that section 631.70, Florida Statutes (2022), did not bar fees because the guaranty association denied a portion of the claim 'by affirmative action, other than delay.' Distinguishing prior decisions in which the association was sued before it could investigate and was compelled to answer, the court noted that here the association was substituted into pending litigation, had the benefit of an automatic stay and two agreed extensions, and then voluntarily pleaded coverage-based affirmative defenses. The court identified a sustained course of conduct constituting affirmative denial: the pre-answer partial payment excluding ordinance-and-law line items, the coverage affirmative defenses, corporate-representative testimony that the claim was not covered, the pretrial stipulation, and a summary judgment motion asserting non-coverage. It also held that where the association is substituted mid-litigation, the relevant inquiry is whether it denied coverage by affirmative action at any point before retrial, not before suit was filed, and that post-answer litigation conduct may be considered. Why it matters: It clarifies how the 'denial by affirmative action' requirement applies when a guaranty association is substituted into pending litigation, including that post-answer litigation positions and partial claim payments can supply the affirmative denial. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10945798/samuel-vainberg-and-lynn-vainberg-v-florida-insurance-guaranty-association/

item.title: Mt. Hawley Insurance Company v. H&M Builders, LLC (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: An insurer sought a declaratory judgment that it owed no duty to defend or indemnify its insured in an underlying state-court wrongful death action, and the district court granted summary judgment to the insured on the duty to defend while reserving the indemnity question. While the insurer's interlocutory appeal was pending, the underlying state-court action settled and was dismissed. The Eleventh Circuit held the appeal no longer presented an actual controversy under the Declaratory Judgment Act and Article III, because a duty-to-defend dispute depends on an actual dispute over a present defense obligation, and it rejected the parties' arguments that potential recovery of defense costs on reversal or of attorney fees under Florida law on affirmance preserved a live dispute, noting also that parties cannot stipulate to federal jurisdiction. Why it matters: It establishes that a duty-to-defend declaratory action becomes moot once the underlying action is settled and dismissed, and that the prospect of recouping defense costs or obtaining a fee award does not by itself supply a live controversy. Also: As an independent ground, the court held that a partial summary judgment order resolving a duty-to-defend claim is appealable under 28 U.S.C. section 1292(a)(1) only if the order has injunctive qualities, examined case by case from the order's language and the parties' claims and counterclaims. Examples include language mandating that the insurer provide a defense or pay defense costs, a ruling on an insurer's request for injunctive relief, or a ruling on an insured's counterclaim for declaratory or injunctive relief. Here the order contained no mandatory language directed at the insurer, the insurer sought no injunctive relief, and the insured filed no counterclaim, so there was no interlocutory jurisdiction. The court expressly declined to follow the unpublished Addison Insurance decision to the extent it could be read to treat any partial summary judgment order on the duty to defend as immediately appealable. Why it matters: It clarifies when an interlocutory coverage ruling on the duty to defend may be appealed before final judgment, limiting section 1292(a)(1) appeals to orders with injunctive qualities. Also: As a third independent ground, the court noted that the district court had since dismissed the duty-to-indemnify claim as moot and entered final judgment, so any appeal was properly taken from that final judgment, into which prior non-final rulings merged. A concurring judge would have rested the dismissal solely on mootness and declined to join the alternative jurisdictional grounds. Why it matters: It confirms that entry of final judgment during a pending interlocutory appeal channels review to an appeal from the final judgment rather than the earlier non-final order. AI-drafted summary. Verify against the opinion. https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/10944729/mt-hawley-insurance-company-v-hm-builders-llc/

item.title: RLI Insurance Company v. Lehman (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: An umbrella insurer sought a declaratory judgment that it owed no coverage for injuries an insured suffered in a car accident, relying on policy language conditioning coverage on the underlying insurance limits being "exhausted by payment of judgments or settlements." One underlying uninsured/underinsured motorist carrier paid its full $200,000 limit, while a second underlying carrier with a $500,000 UM limit initially denied the claim and later settled for $50,001. Applying Florida law and dictionary definitions of "exhaust," the Eleventh Circuit held that a settlement well below the underlying policy limits does not fully consume those limits and therefore does not satisfy the exhaustion clause. The court distinguished a Florida Third District Court of Appeal decision that had found exhaustion through a below-limits settlement, noting that the clause there referred to exhausting "all primary insurance" without reference to policy limits and that the decision did not analyze the plain meaning of "exhaust," and concluded there was persuasive indication the Florida Supreme Court would depart from it. The panel vacated the sua sponte summary judgment entered for the insureds and remanded with instructions to enter judgment for the insurer, without reaching whether the insureds maintained the required amount of underlying UM coverage. item.title: National Assisted Living Risk Retention Group v. Bishop (Fla. DCA)
item.category: District Court of Appeal of Florida
item.description: An assisted living resident wandered from the facility in July 2012 and was killed crossing a highway. The facility manager telephoned the insurance agent to report the death and the ensuing state agency investigations, but no demand or suit was made until the estate filed a wrongful death action in 2014. After obtaining a $20 million judgment and an assignment of the insured's rights under the 2012 claims-made policy through proceedings supplementary, the estate sued the insurer for denying coverage and a defense. Why it matters: The decision draws a clear line under a claims-made policy between reporting an occurrence that may later generate a claim and a claim actually being made, and holds that regulatory investigations and inquiries about proof of insurance do not constitute a claim on behalf of the injured person. Also: The court separately held that the trial court's finding that the insurer failed to prove a valid retroactive cancellation for nonpayment did not resolve the coverage question. Even if the 2012 policy was never properly cancelled, it expired by its own terms in January 2013, so the claim first made in the 2014 wrongful death action fell outside the policy period and any extended discovery period, none of which the insured purchased despite notices offering it. The court declined to reach reformation or estoppel theories directed at the later policies because the estate had voluntarily dismissed those counts with prejudice and had never obtained an assignment of rights under them. item.title: City of Brunswick v. Honeywell International, Inc. (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: A city sued two companies in Georgia state court for continuing nuisance and continuing trespass based on pollution around a Superfund site; the defendants removed under the federal officer removal statute, 28 U.S.C. section 1442(a)(1), and the district court remanded. While the appeal of the remand order was pending, the parties litigated in state court and the city amended its complaint twice, and the city argued the appeal was moot. Applying the Griggs principle as explained in Coinbase, the court held that a timely notice of appeal from a remand order reviewable under 28 U.S.C. section 1447(d) automatically stays all district court proceedings, including the remand order itself, so that later state court proceedings are void for purposes of the appeal, and that the earlier mailing of the remand order to the state court does not defeat the stay because the district court retains jurisdiction to reconsider a reviewable remand order. The court denied the city's motion to dismiss and rejected the mootness argument based on the amended state court complaints. Why it matters: It establishes in the Eleventh Circuit that an appeal from a remand order in a federal officer removal case operates as a self-executing stay of district court proceedings, so post-remand state court activity and amended pleadings do not affect appellate review, a position that diverges from the Ninth Circuit's discretionary-stay approach and aligns with the Fourth Circuit. Also: As an alternative ground for denying the motion to dismiss, the court held that the defendants did not waive their right to remove or to appeal the remand order by answering, moving to dismiss, and appearing at a hearing in state court after remand. Waiver principles reach substantial offensive or defensive action taken in state court before removal, and here the only conduct identified occurred after remand and after the plaintiff itself successfully asked the state court to lift its stay pending appeal. Under those circumstances the defendants had no practical choice but to participate. Why it matters: It clarifies that post-remand participation in state court litigation, particularly where the plaintiff obtained dissolution of a stay pending appeal, does not forfeit the right to appeal a remand order. Also: On the merits, the court held that removal under 28 U.S.C. section 1442(a)(1) was proper. The defendants were "acting under" the EPA because, unlike an ordinary regulated party merely complying with detailed regulation, they were carrying out remediation selected in an EPA Record of Decision and consent decree at a listed Superfund site, work the agency would otherwise have had to perform; the city's continuing nuisance and trespass claims premised on inadequate remediation were "for or relating to" those acts; and the defendants raised a colorable federal defense that CERCLA and the consent decree conflict-preempt the state tort remedies. The court also stated that, following the Supreme Court's Plaquemines Parish decision, the "causal connection" and "causal nexus" phrasing previously used for the second prong should be retired in favor of asking whether the challenged acts are closely connected to the performance of federal duties. Why it matters: It clarifies when parties performing EPA-directed CERCLA cleanup may remove state tort suits to federal court and updates the Eleventh Circuit's articulation of the "for or relating to" prong of the federal officer removal test. item.title: The Town of Pine Hill, Alabama v. 3M Company (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: A municipal water provider sued a chemical manufacturer in Alabama state court on state-law negligence, wantonness, nuisance, and trespass theories for PFAS contamination of its raw water source, and the manufacturer removed under the federal officer removal statute, 28 U.S.C. section 1442(a)(1). The district court remanded, reasoning that the gravamen of the claims was the sale of PFAS products to private paper mills, conduct not undertaken under color of federal office. The Eleventh Circuit held that the first prong of the removal test was satisfied, reading its prior decision that section 1442(a)(1) reaches only current officers as addressed to removal of a state criminal prosecution and not as barring a contractor sued civilly for past conduct performed while assisting a federal superior. The court found the manufacturer's notice of removal sufficiently alleged that it acted under a federal officer in producing firefighting foam to detailed military specifications, and vacated the remand order. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a company sued civilly for conduct performed years earlier while assisting a federal officer may still invoke federal officer removal, limiting the reach of the court's prior holding that the statute covers only current officers. Also: On the second prong, the court held that the district court should have credited the removing defendant's theory of the case and identified the gravamen of the complaint as overall PFAS contamination of the river rather than only sales to paper mills. Addressing an issue it said it had not previously decided, the court adopted the First Circuit's framework distinguishing express disclaimers that fully eliminate any ground for federal officer removal from artful pleading, and held that a disclaimer requiring a state court to determine the nexus between the charged conduct and federal authority does not defeat removal. It concluded the plaintiff's disclaimer of relief for aqueous film forming foam contamination amounted to artful pleading because commingled contamination from a nearby air base was plausibly alleged. Why it matters: It establishes in the Eleventh Circuit that a plaintiff's express disclaimer of federally connected claims can sever the causal nexus for federal officer removal only if it wholly removes the federal question from the case, and that a disclaimer leaving a state court to sort out the federal nexus does not. Also: On the third prong, the court held that the notice of removal plausibly alleged a colorable government contractor defense under the Boyle elements, pointing to allegations of reasonably precise military specifications, inclusion on a Department of Defense qualified products list, and government knowledge of the relevant hazards. Because the challenge to removal was facial, the court limited its review to the complaint and the notice of removal and declined to consider a multidistrict litigation court's summary judgment ruling on the same defense. It emphasized that the defense need only be plausible and that its ultimate validity is not decided at the removal stage. Why it matters: It confirms that a facial challenge to a notice of removal is assessed on the complaint and notice alone and that a government contractor defense need only be plausible, not proven, to support federal officer removal. item.title: Michael Davis v. Lockheed Martin Corporation (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: Plaintiffs in two coordinated toxic-tort cases alleged that volatile organic compounds released from a manufacturing facility caused multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's, and other neurodegenerative diseases, and they offered two general-causation experts. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed exclusion of the first expert, holding that a district court does not abuse its discretion in finding a 'weight of the evidence' causation opinion unreliable where the expert failed to explain how he searched, sorted, and weighed the literature or ranked rival explanations, and separately failed to analyze the Bradford Hill factors in more than a conclusory sentence applied to a single study. Joining the First, Third, Sixth, and Seventh Circuits, the court held that an expert using the weight-of-the-evidence method must explain how he weighed the evidence, and that although the Bradford Hill factors are not always required, a court may require an expert who invokes them to address each in some depth. With no admissible general-causation testimony, summary judgment for the defendant was affirmed. Why it matters: The decision sets binding Circuit guidance on what a general-causation expert must show to survive Rule 702 review in toxic-tort litigation, specifically that the weight-of-the-evidence methodology must be explained rather than asserted and that a cursory Bradford Hill discussion can support exclusion. Also: The court separately affirmed exclusion of the plaintiffs' second expert on two independent grounds. His general-causation opinion was unreliable because it merely adopted other experts' reports and 'the science' without explaining any methodology of his own, which the court characterized as the ipse dixit an expert may not substitute for analysis. His second opinion was not a valid background-risk assessment because it rested on a statistician's comparison of mortality rates in a zip code near the facility to rates in more distant areas, rather than comparing disease rates in exposed and unexposed populations, and neither expert knew the actual exposure levels of the compared groups. Why it matters: It clarifies that an expert cannot establish general causation by wholesale adoption of another expert's report, and it specifies that a background-risk methodology requires a comparison of disease rates between exposed and unexposed populations with known exposure levels, not a geographic proxy based on mortality data. Also: Addressing appellate jurisdiction, the court held the district court did not abuse its discretion in certifying under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b) a partial summary judgment that resolved all claims of a subset of plaintiffs in a multi-plaintiff case. The judgment was final as to those plaintiffs even though other plaintiffs' claims remained, and those remaining claims involved different illnesses unrelated to the general-causation evidence at issue. The court found no just reason for delay because the certified appeal raised the same issues, on a materially identical order, as a companion appeal, so requiring the plaintiffs to wait would force two identical appeals. Why it matters: It illustrates the standards for Rule 54(b) certification in multi-plaintiff mass-tort litigation, including that separability of the remaining claims and avoidance of duplicative appeals can support immediate review of a partial summary judgment. item.title: Patel v. Brim (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Plaintiffs sued a farm owner for negligence and under the Georgia Dram Shop Act after an underage guest became intoxicated at a graduation party on the property and then crashed a vehicle off the premises, injuring a passenger. Plaintiffs conceded the owner did not sell, furnish, or serve the alcohol, which underage attendees brought themselves, but argued liability should attach because he knew or should have known of the underage drinking and took no steps to prevent it or to stop intoxicated guests from driving. The Court of Appeals held that OCGA 51-1-40 is the exclusive remedy for claims against a third person arising from an intoxicated person's acts, that subsection (b) reaches only one who furnishes the alcohol itself and not one who merely furnishes the premises where alcohol is consumed, and that because the Act is in derogation of the common law it cannot be extended beyond its plain terms. The trial court's dismissal under OCGA 9-11-12(b)(6) was affirmed. Why it matters: The decision reaffirms that a premises owner who does not sell, furnish, or serve alcohol has no exposure under the Dram Shop Act, and that the Act displaces common-law theories such as failure to supervise minors or failure to prevent an intoxicated guest from driving. Also: The court separately rejected the argument that OCGA 51-1-40(d), which shields an owner, lessee, or lawful occupant from liability when alcohol is consumed on the premises in the owner's absence and without consent, implies a cause of action where the owner impliedly consented to the consumption. Applying plain-meaning construction, the court held that subsection (d) is clear in insulating owners in the described circumstances and is otherwise silent, and that reading contrapositive clauses into it would render meaningless subsection (a)'s declaration that consumption, not furnishing, is the proximate cause of injury except as provided in subsection (b). The court concluded that the legislature could have created an implied-consent exception in subsection (b) and did not. Why it matters: The opinion establishes that subsection (d) is purely an immunity provision and cannot be inverted to create liability based on a property owner's alleged implied consent to drinking on the premises. item.title: Keais v. Kelley (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: A cyclist was struck and killed by a driver who fled the scene and instead summoned a non-driver, an attorney, who observed the scene and made informal calls rather than contacting emergency services. The trial court dismissed the wrongful death claim against the non-driver on the ground that the render-aid and reporting duties of OCGA 40-6-270 apply only to the driver. The Court of Appeals agreed that the statutory duties in OCGA 40-6-270 bind only the driver of the vehicle, but held that a non-driver who voluntarily undertakes those duties may be liable under the voluntary undertaking doctrine of Restatement (Second) of Torts Section 324A, extending Carmichael beyond premises and inspection contexts to a non-delegable statutory duty. Because the complaint alleged the non-driver assumed control of the incident and negligently handled reporting, dismissal was improper at the pleading stage. Why it matters: The decision confirms that OCGA 40-6-270's stop-and-render-aid duties apply only to the driver while holding that a non-driver who voluntarily undertakes those duties can face wrongful death liability under Restatement Section 324A, extending the voluntary undertaking doctrine to statutory motor-vehicle duties. Also: The court addressed its own jurisdiction over the plaintiff's appeal from the order granting the non-driver's motion to dismiss, which was not a final judgment because claims against other defendants remained pending and no OCGA 9-11-54(b) certificate was entered. The court held that because it had granted a co-defendant's application for interlocutory review and that appeal was properly before it, the plaintiff's earlier-filed notice of appeal ripened and was reviewable as a cross appeal under OCGA 5-6-38. Why it matters: It clarifies that an appeal from a non-final dismissal order that would otherwise require interlocutory procedures may be entertained as a cross appeal when a co-party's interlocutory appeal from the same litigation is properly pending. Also: The court analyzed whether the renewal action under OCGA 9-2-61 involved substantially the same parties as the original federal action, examining the case captions of the pleadings and the dismissal order. It held that because the district court's dismissal order still listed the plaintiff in both his individual and representative capacities and nothing showed he had been dropped in his individual capacity, the parties were substantially the same and the renewal was valid. Why it matters: It reaffirms that renewal-action party identity under OCGA 9-2-61 is assessed by reference to the case captions of the pleadings and dismissal order, and that a plaintiff is not treated as dropped absent a record showing of dismissal in that capacity. Also: The court held that Georgia's Wrongful Death Act establishes a strict standing hierarchy, spouse, then children, then parents, then the estate's administrator, under OCGA 51-4-2, 51-4-4, 51-4-5, and 19-7-1. Because the decedent left no spouse or children, the parent had standing to sue individually under OCGA 51-4-4 and therefore could not also maintain the action as administrator of the estate. The trial court's denial of dismissal as to the administrator capacity was reversed. Why it matters: It confirms that a parent with individual standing to bring a wrongful death claim cannot simultaneously sue as administrator of the decedent's estate under the Act's exclusive standing hierarchy. item.description: In an auto negligence case where the jury awarded the plaintiff $250,000, the trial court awarded the plaintiff attorney fees and expenses under OCGA § 9-11-68 after the plaintiff beat her rejected settlement offer. The court found the offeree failed to carry that burden where she pointed only to a modest discrepancy between alleged and proven medical damages and an unspecified denial of medical records. Why it matters: The decision reaffirms that the good-faith inquiry under the offer-of-settlement statute turns on the offeror's subjective beliefs and places the burden on the offeree to disprove good faith. Also: The court held that a contingency fee agreement may be considered as evidence of usual and customary fees, but an award cannot rest on the contingency agreement alone; the party seeking fees must also introduce evidence of hours, rates, or some other indication of the value of services rendered. The award was properly supported here because counsel testified about his experience, hourly rate, and the work performed, and submitted detailed work logs, and the court awarded less than the amount requested. Why it matters: It clarifies that a contingency fee agreement is admissible but insufficient by itself to support a fee award under OCGA § 9-11-68 absent additional evidence of hours and rates. Also: The court held that an award under OCGA § 9-11-68(b)(2) is limited to reasonable attorney fees and expenses incurred from the date the offer of settlement was rejected through entry of judgment. The record showed the fees awarded were limited to work performed after the offer's expiration, as reflected in counsel's affidavit, work logs, and the trial court's express limitation to post-expiration work. Why it matters: It confirms that recoverable fees under the offer-of-settlement statute are confined to work performed after rejection of the offer. AI-drafted summary. item.title: Master Dry Out, Inc., a/a/o Abijana v. State Farm Florida Insurance Company (Fla. DCA)
item.category: District Court of Appeal of Florida
item.description: An assignee of residential property insurance benefits sued the insurer for breach of contract, settled the case with an express disclaimer of liability and a recital that the agreement compromised doubtful and disputed claims, dismissed the suit, and then moved for attorney's fees under section 627.7152(10)(a), Florida Statutes, arguing the settlement was the functional equivalent of a confession of judgment. The Second District held that the statute permits fees only based on the difference between the 'judgment obtained' and the presuit settlement offer, and that section 627.7152(1)(e) defines 'judgment obtained' as damages recovered. Applying the principle that settlement dollars are not synonymous with damages, the court concluded the settlement was not a 'judgment obtained' and affirmed the denial of fees. Why it matters: The decision construes the assignment-of-benefits fee provision to require an actual judgment, so a negotiated settlement without an admission of liability does not itself support a fee award under section 627.7152(10)(a). item.title: Monsanto Co. v. Durnell (U.S.)
item.category: Supreme Court of the United States
item.description: Plaintiff brought a state-law failure-to-warn tort claim alleging that the manufacturer of a glyphosate-based herbicide should have included a cancer warning on its label, and a jury awarded damages. The Court held that FIFRA's preemption clause, 7 U.S.C. section 136v(b), expressly preempts that claim because EPA approved the product's label without a cancer warning and federal law requires the manufacturer to use the EPA-approved label, so a state tort duty to add a cancer warning would impose a labeling requirement 'in addition to or different from' the federal requirement. The Court reasoned that EPA's registration and labeling determinations impose 'requirements' under FIFRA, relying on Riegel v. Medtronic, and rejected arguments that 7 U.S.C. section 136a(f)(2) preserved parallel state misbranding-based claims. Why it matters: It resolves a circuit split, including the Eleventh Circuit's contrary decision in Carson v. Monsanto, by holding that FIFRA expressly preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims premised on a missing cancer warning where EPA approved the label without one, directly affecting glyphosate products-liability litigation in Georgia and the Eleventh Circuit. item.title: Scott v. Evans Delivery Company, Inc. (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In a wrongful death action arising from a tractor-trailer collision, the trial court granted summary judgment to the defendant trucking company and driver, holding that the avoidable consequences doctrine under OCGA section 51-11-7 barred recovery because dashcam video conclusively showed the decedent failed to exercise ordinary care for his own safety. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding that the grainy and disjointed dashcam video did not clearly and unambiguously depict what the decedent should have perceived, so it could not be given conclusive weight under the Scott v. Harris standard. The court held that ambiguities in video evidence, like any other material fact, must be construed in the nonmoving party's favor, and that whether a plaintiff exercised ordinary care for his own safety and to avoid the consequences of another's negligence is ordinarily a jury question except in plain, palpable, and undisputed cases. Why it matters: It clarifies that video evidence can be given conclusive weight at summary judgment only when it clearly and unambiguously depicts the event, and that ambiguous or low-quality footage must be construed in favor of the nonmovant rather than treated as dispositive. item.title: Onsite Communication Services, LLC v. Gooch (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: After a head-on collision, the defendant driver, his employer, and the employer's insurer each moved for summary judgment on negligence per se, direct negligence, punitive damages, attorney fees, and the propriety of a direct action against the insurer. The Court of Appeals held that the driver's admitted habitual methamphetamine use, his unexplained crossing of the centerline, and a positive drug test the day after the collision created a jury question on whether he was impaired at the time of the collision, even where other opinion evidence suggested he was not impaired. The court affirmed denial of summary judgment. Why it matters: The decision confirms that a positive post-collision drug test, habitual drug use, and an unexplained traffic violation can together create a jury question on driver impairment notwithstanding contrary opinion testimony. Also: The driver and employer argued the negligence per se claims based on the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations failed because the driver operated entirely intrastate. The court held that at the time of the collision Georgia had adopted the FMCSR as its own safety regulations applicable to intrastate commerce under Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 515-16-4-.01, interpreting references to interstate commerce as intrastate commerce in Georgia, and that the complaint's substance encompassed that adoption even though it cited only the FMCSR. Why it matters: The opinion clarifies that Georgia's adoption of the FMCSR extends those regulations to intrastate drivers, allowing negligence per se claims to proceed without an interstate nexus. Also: The employer challenged the direct negligence claims and the punitive damages and attorney fees claims. The court held that evidence the employer had actual or constructive knowledge of the driver's drug use and multiple speeding tickets while driving company trucks yet took no action created jury questions on negligent training, supervision, and retention, and that the same evidence, combined with the impairment issue, supported submission of punitive damages under OCGA § 51-12-5.1 (b) and attorney fees under OCGA § 13-6-11. Why it matters: The decision confirms that an employer's inaction despite knowledge of a driver's drug use and traffic violations can support direct negligence, punitive damages, and attorney fees claims beyond a mere rule-of-the-road violation. Also: The insurer argued the direct action against it was unauthorized because its insured was not a for-hire motor carrier. The court held that the plain language of OCGA § 40-2-140 (d) (4) (2021) authorizes a direct action against the insurer of any motor carrier and is not limited to for-hire motor carriers, rejecting the insurer's attempt to import the for-hire intrastate motor carrier language from a separate subsection. Why it matters: The opinion construes the pre-2024 version of Georgia's direct-action statute to permit suit against the insurer of any motor carrier, not only for-hire carriers. AI-drafted summary. item.title: Ortho Sport & Spine Physicians, LLC v. Snowden (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In a personal injury suit arising from an automobile collision, a non-party medical provider challenged trial court orders compelling production of database reports and other materials related to its billing for other patients, sought to test the reasonableness of the plaintiff's medical charges. The Court of Appeals held that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in ordering three eClinicalWorks reports rather than one, because the provider's billing system necessitated multiple reports to obtain the information permitted by the court's prior opinion. The court vacated the order to the extent it inconsistently addressed whether patient identification or account numbers and payor names could be redacted, and remanded for clarification. Why it matters: It clarifies the permissible scope of third-party discovery into a medical provider's billing data (charges, write-offs, adjustments, and payments accepted from other patients) used to assess the reasonableness of a plaintiff's medical charges and confirms a trial court may order multiple database reports when the provider's system makes a single report impractical. Also: The court addressed whether the provider could be compelled to hand-review emails or files to compile lists of patients meeting certain criteria. It reaffirmed that a non-party cannot be required to create a document that does not exist simply for discovery purposes, though it may be tasked with extracting and translating data from an existing electronic database into reasonably usable form. The court vacated the show cause order's hand-review requirement to the extent it imposed a duty to create a non-existent document and remanded for the trial court to clarify the scope of that requirement. Why it matters: It draws a line under OCGA section 9-11-34(a) between compelling a non-party to extract data from an existing database, which is permissible, and compelling it to create a new document that does not exist, which is not. item.title: Cook v. SMG Construction Services, LLC (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: On remand from the Supreme Court of Georgia, which held that plaintiff had actual knowledge as a matter of law of an unguarded balcony ledge in a house under construction, the Court of Appeals addressed the remaining elements of the landowner's affirmative defenses of assumption of the risk and voluntary negligence. The court held that although the actual-knowledge and appreciation-of-risk elements of assumption of the risk were established, a genuine issue of material fact existed on the voluntary-exposure element, because the standard is subjective and there was evidence that environmental conditions such as drywall dust, overspray, poor lighting, and lack of visual contrast impaired plaintiff's perception of the ledge's exact location. The court reasoned that perception before plaintiff turned away and walked backward was material to whether he deliberately chose to expose himself to the risk. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that the voluntary-exposure element of assumption of the risk is a subjective, fact-specific inquiry that can present a jury question even where actual knowledge of the hazard is established as a matter of law, and that conditions impairing perception of a hazard's exact location are material to that inquiry. Also: The court separately held that the landowner was not entitled to summary judgment on its affirmative defense of voluntary negligence. Voluntary negligence requires that the plaintiff purposefully place himself within reach of the danger, and a failure to exercise reasonable attention to surroundings is not enough. A genuine issue of material fact existed as to whether plaintiff purposefully put himself within reach of the unguarded ledge, given evidence that the bathroom where he was working was not near the ledge and that he could not accurately perceive its proximity. Why it matters: It clarifies that voluntary negligence requires a purposeful exposure to the known danger and is not established merely by inattention, leaving the question for the jury on these facts. item.title: Cecilia Vera v. Parkwood Condominium Association, Inc. (Fla. DCA)
item.category: District Court of Appeal of Florida
item.description: A condominium unit owner slipped on water and sewage from a wastewater backup inside her own unit's bathroom and sued the association and its management company for premises liability, relying on Florida's transient-substance line of cases and evidence of recurring backups reported to the association. The Third District held that line of authority did not control because the fall occurred inside the unit, which the association did not solely possess or control, and because the backup could have originated in either the unit's plumbing, which the owner was responsible to maintain, or the building's sanitary stack pipes, which the association maintained. Because every deponent, including the plaintiff, her adult children, and the association's corporate representative, testified they did not know the source of the blockage, the plaintiff failed to produce evidence supporting a reasonable inference that it was more likely than not that the association's pipes caused the spillage. Summary judgment for the association was affirmed. Why it matters: The decision marks the limits of the transient-substance and notice framework by requiring, where a hazard could have arisen from plumbing maintained by either the unit owner or the association, evidence making it more likely than not that the component under the defendant's control caused the condition. item.title: Universal Property & Casualty Insurance Company v. Orlando Cisneros Dameras (Fla. DCA)
item.category: District Court of Appeal of Florida
item.description: After a settlement in a first-party property insurance case, the trial court awarded the insured a lodestar fee of $389,362.50 enhanced by a 2.5 contingency risk multiplier, for a total of $973,406.25, plus costs. The Third District affirmed the lodestar computation as supported by sufficient findings under Rowe and Quanstrom, but reversed the multiplier because the record contained no competent substantial evidence on the first Quanstrom factor. The court explained that counsel's own skill, experience, and willingness to try the case does not address whether other competent attorneys in the relevant market would have taken the case without the availability of a multiplier, and the fee expert's assertion that the case was risky and that "nobody" would take it did not supply that proof, particularly where the trial court acknowledged that numerous other south Florida property insurance firms could have obtained some recovery. The court remanded for entry of the lodestar without any multiplier. Why it matters: The decision reiterates and applies the evidentiary showing required before a contingency fee multiplier may be added to a lodestar award in insurance fee litigation, specifically proof about the availability of other competent counsel in the relevant market absent a multiplier. Also: The court also reversed the $42,658.25 cost award for the fees of two expert witnesses who were retained to prepare the case for trial but did not testify. Such costs are governed by section 92.231(2), Florida Statutes, which authorizes taxing costs for "[a]ny expert or skilled witness who shall have testified in any cause," and costs are taxable only where authorized by statute or rule. The court noted the narrow exception under which trial-preparation fees may be awarded when the expert testimony was reasonably necessary for trial, but found the record contained no such findings. On remand the trial court must conduct an appropriate analysis, make findings based on the evidence presented, and omit any fees for non-testifying experts not reasonably necessary for trial preparation. Why it matters: It confirms that fees for retained experts who never testify are not taxable as costs under section 92.231(2) absent express findings that the preparation was reasonably necessary for trial, a recurring cost-award question in first-party property insurance litigation. item.title: Wal-Mart Stores East, LP v. Johnson (Fla. DCA)
item.category: District Court of Appeal of Florida
item.description: An independent contractor's service technician was injured when he touched an ungrounded, non-NEC-compliant metal junction box in a Wal-Mart store and was shocked, causing him to fall from a ladder. Wal-Mart asserted the independent contractor defense, arguing it owed no duty because it did not control the means and methods of the work and lacked knowledge of any dangerous condition. The Second DCA affirmed the denial of Wal-Mart's motions for summary judgment and directed verdict, holding that the second exception to the no-liability rule applied because the evidence supported that Wal-Mart had constructive knowledge of a concealed dangerous condition it negligently created or approved. The court emphasized that the box was in a locked, key-card-restricted area accessible only to Wal-Mart personnel, that the breakers were unlabeled, that the danger was concealed and not inherent in the door-installation work, and that the technician reasonably expected the box to be safe to touch. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a property owner cannot invoke the independent contractor defense where the owner had actual or constructive knowledge of a concealed dangerous condition it negligently created, even absent control over the contractor's work methods, and applies the constructive-knowledge-of-concealed-danger exception in detail. item.title: QuikTrip Corporation v. Robinson (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Plaintiff sued for injuries from a sidewalk trip and fall at defendant's store. The defendant removed the case on diversity grounds, plaintiff obtained a remand by arguing the amount in controversy was unclear, and after remand a doctor issued a permanent impairment rating. The Court of Appeals held that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in declining to apply judicial estoppel to cap damages at $75,000, because the post-remand permanent impairment rating constituted a change in circumstances under Wal-Mart Stores E., LP v. Howell, and because it was not conclusively established that plaintiff had taken a clearly inconsistent position in federal court. Why it matters: The decision applies and reinforces the rule that a post-remand change in circumstances affecting damages, such as a later permanent impairment rating, defeats judicial estoppel even where a plaintiff obtained remand by minimizing the amount in controversy. Also: The defendant argued the $1.8 million award was arbitrary and excessive for what it characterized as a broken pinky finger. The court held the award was not so excessive as to be inconsistent with the preponderance of the evidence under OCGA section 51-12-12 (a), citing evidence of a permanent hand fracture at the base of the joint on the dominant hand, surgery, lasting limited range of motion, scarring, and impairment of life activities. The court noted that pain and suffering damages are governed by the enlightened conscience of the jury, are not confined to a multiple of special damages, and may compensate future as well as past suffering. Why it matters: It confirms the heavy burden on a party challenging a pain and suffering award as excessive and that such awards need not be tied to medical specials, even for an injury characterized as minor. Also: The defendant contended the verdict was tainted by closing arguments portraying it as a bad actor that fought responsibility for ten years. The court held the challenge was not preserved because the defendant did not object contemporaneously, and added that the arguments fell within legitimate comment and did not constitute an improper request for the jury to punish the defendant. Why it matters: It reiterates that unobjected-to closing argument is not preserved for review and that comment on a party's resistance to responsibility can be legitimate argument rather than an improper call to punish.
