item.title: Douglas v. Bhakta (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In an auto-accident suit, defendant admitted in his answer that he was a Kansas resident at the time of the accident and at the time of suit but did not assert insufficiency of service of process by motion filed before or simultaneously with the answer. The Court of Appeals held that a defendant waives the defense of insufficiency of service of process under OCGA section 9-11-12(h)(1)(B) by failing to raise it in the original answer or a contemporaneously filed motion, and that a general reference to lack of personal jurisdiction does not preserve the service defense. The court further held that, because defendant admitted out-of-state residency in his answer, he was subject to service under the Nonresident Motorist Act, and his later conclusory affidavit asserting Georgia residency could not overcome that binding judicial admission, which he never moved to withdraw. The court also clarified that a nonresident defendant involved in a Georgia accident is subject to jurisdiction under the NRMA when nonresident at both the time of accident and time of suit, while the Long Arm Statute applies when the defendant was a Georgia resident at the time of the accident and later became a nonresident. The dismissal was reversed. Why it matters: It clarifies that the service-of-process defense in NRMA auto cases must be raised in the original answer or a simultaneously filed motion or it is waived, and that an answer admission of residency is a binding judicial admission that a later self-serving affidavit cannot overcome absent a motion to withdraw. Also: The trial court had granted defendant's motion to withdraw deemed admissions under OCGA section 9-11-36(b), including admissions concerning residence. Following its holding in Division 1, the Court of Appeals reversed the withdrawal as to the residency-related requests because defendant had admitted Kansas residency and failed to preserve the service defense, but found no abuse of discretion as to the remaining requests and directed that discovery be reopened on remand in light of newly provided eyewitness evidence. Why it matters: It illustrates that withdrawal of deemed admissions under OCGA section 9-11-36(b) cannot be used to undo a binding pleading admission that controls a dispositive jurisdictional issue. item.title: Yamaha Motor Manufacturing Corporation of America v. Hall (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: In a products-liability action arising from a golf cart rollover, the trial court excluded the specific contents of the manufacturer's warning labels and operator's manual, allowing only evidence that warnings existed and how they were delivered. The Court of Appeals held that the contents of the warnings were relevant and admissible to the risk-utility analysis on the design-defect claim under the Banks 'efficacy of warnings' factor, even though those contents were inadmissible on the communication-based failure-to-warn claim because the operator never read them. The court reasoned that evidence inadmissible for one purpose may be admissible for another and that the error was not harmless, and it rejected the contention that the manufacturer waived the argument by not using the phrase 'risk-utility analysis' below. Why it matters: It clarifies that the contents of a manufacturer's warnings are admissible on the design-defect risk-utility analysis under Banks even when those contents are inadmissible on a failure-to-warn claim, and confirms that no magic words are required to preserve a relevance argument. Also: The manufacturer argued for the first time on appeal that it owed no duty to ensure its warning labels and operator's manual remained with the golf cart through the product's life cycle. The court held the argument was not preserved because, under OCGA section 9-11-50 (a), a directed-verdict motion must state its specific grounds, and the manufacturer never raised the absence of a duty when it moved for a directed verdict below, having instead argued only the adequacy of communication and proximate cause. Why it matters: It reinforces that a ground for directed verdict not specifically stated in the trial court motion cannot be raised for the first time on appeal. Also: The manufacturer invited the court to revisit AU Medical Center v. Dale, in which a plurality held that the term 'brought' in the former version of OCGA section 51-12-33 (b) refers to the number of named defendants remaining at the time of trial, which had led the trial court to enter the full judgment against the manufacturer despite the jury allocating fault to dismissed non-parties. The court declined the invitation to revisit that holding. Why it matters: It signals that the court will not reconsider its apportionment construction in AU Medical Center v. Dale regarding allocation of fault to dismissed non-parties under the former statute. AI-drafted summary. item.title: T. M. v. University of Maryland Medical System Corporation (U.S.)
item.category: Supreme Court of the United States
item.description: The Supreme Court held that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal district court jurisdiction over cases brought by state-court losers complaining of injuries caused by state-court judgments rendered before the federal proceedings commenced and seeking district court review and rejection of those judgments, regardless of whether the state-court judgment remains subject to further review in state appellate proceedings. The Court rejected the argument that the doctrine applies only to final judgments rendered by the highest court of a State, reasoning that the doctrine rests on the functional distinction between original and appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. sections 1331 and 1257, not solely on a negative inference from section 1257. Petitioner had sued in federal court to declare a state consent order unconstitutional and unenforceable while simultaneously appealing it in state court. The Court resolved a conflict among the Courts of Appeals. Why it matters: The decision clarifies the scope of a threshold jurisdictional doctrine and confirms that Rooker-Feldman can bar a federal suit even when the underlying state-court judgment is still on appeal, which directly affects civil litigants pursuing parallel state and federal proceedings. item.title: Lloyd v. City of Atlanta (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Plaintiff, injured when his bike tire became lodged in a city storm drain grate, sent an ante litem notice jointly addressed to the City of Atlanta and Fulton County demanding a "global settlement amount" of $2,000,000. The Court of Appeals held that this notice failed to comply with OCGA section 36-33-5(e), which requires a specific amount of monetary damages being sought from the municipal corporation, because demanding a single global amount from two entities jointly does not identify the specific amount sought from the city alone and leaves the city to speculate what portion constituted an offer it could accept. The court noted it need not decide whether subsection (e) requires strict or substantial compliance because the notice failed under either standard, and rejected the argument that use of "and/or" cured the defect, finding the term was used only to reference the applicable notice statutes. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that an ante litem notice presenting a single combined settlement demand against a municipality and another governmental entity, without specifying the amount sought from the municipality alone, fails the specific-amount requirement of OCGA section 36-33-5(e) and bars suit as a condition precedent. item.title: Cayamcela v. Advocacy Trust, LLC (Ga.)
item.description: In a medical malpractice and wrongful death action arising from a patient's death in the ICU after childbirth, the jury returned a $42 million verdict against a doctor and a medical staffing agency. The Supreme Court of Georgia affirmed the trial court's exclusion under OCGA section 24-7-702(b) of a defense expert's testimony about ICU care, holding the court acted within its gatekeeping discretion where the expert repeatedly admitted he had not reviewed the relevant ICU records well enough to opine on that care and that the matter fell outside his specialty. The court rejected the argument that these gaps went only to credibility rather than admissibility. Why it matters: The decision confirms that a trial court may exclude expert testimony as unreliable under Rule 702(b) when the expert concedes an insufficient factual basis, and that such deficiencies bear on admissibility, not merely weight. Also: The court held that the noneconomic damages cap of OCGA section 51-13-1(b) could not be constitutionally applied to the jury's verdict. Relying on its companion decision in Clark v. Leigh, issued the same day, the court reaffirmed that stare decisis preserves Nestlehutt and that where any part of a medical malpractice award is for noneconomic damages subject to the right to a jury trial, the cap cannot be applied without violating that right. Why it matters: The ruling confirms that the medical malpractice noneconomic damages cap remains unenforceable as applied to jury verdicts that include noneconomic damages, leaving Nestlehutt intact and extending its reasoning to wrongful death awards. Also: The court held that the defendants affirmatively waived their challenge to a jury instruction stating that defendants bore the burden of proof on whether other medical professionals were the sole proximate cause. By proposing the opposite instruction, then withdrawing all proposed instructions, and stating multiple times that they had no objection to the court's charge, the defendants waived even substantial-error review under OCGA section 5-5-24(c). Why it matters: The decision clarifies that affirmative waiver, by withdrawing requested instructions and acquiescing in the charge given, forecloses substantial-error review of an instructional error on appeal. Also: The court affirmed the roughly $11.8 million attorney fee award under OCGA section 9-11-68, holding the plaintiffs' settlement offer satisfied subsection (a)(7) because it stated plaintiffs would pay their own fees and expenses, which were incurred for the claims rather than part of them. The court further held that OCGA section 9-15-16 and Couch bar use of a contingency fee agreement to prove the reasonableness of fees but do not bar considering the agreement for other purposes, such as proving total fees incurred, and that the trial court properly established reasonableness through other evidence. Why it matters: The decision clarifies that a contingency fee agreement may be used to establish total fees incurred even though it cannot prove their reasonableness under OCGA section 9-15-16, and addresses what satisfies the offer requirements of OCGA section 9-11-68(a)(7). item.title: Clark v. Leigh (Ga.)
item.description: In a medical malpractice and wrongful death action where a jury awarded $29,250,000 for the full value of the decedent's life, $2,500,000 for pain and suffering, and medical expenses, the trial court applied the OCGA section 51-13-1(b) noneconomic damages cap to reduce the wrongful death award to $350,000. The Supreme Court of Georgia reaffirmed Nestlehutt, holding that the right to trial by jury under the Georgia Constitution does not permit applying the cap to pain and suffering and loss of consortium damages in medical malpractice actions, and declined to overrule it under stare decisis. The court then held that, under ordinary principles of statutory construction and in light of Nestlehutt, the cap statute cannot operate at all on a judgment in a case like this one, where the jury's verdict includes noneconomic damages for a cause of action to which the jury trial right applies, because making it operative would require impermissibly rewriting the statute. The court vacated the order applying the cap and remanded for the trial court to decide the defendants' excessiveness claim as to the wrongful death award. Why it matters: The decision reaffirms that the OCGA section 51-13-1(b) medical malpractice noneconomic damages cap is unenforceable as to constitutionally protected jury-determined damages and extends that result, on statutory-construction grounds, to render the cap inoperative on the entire judgment including 'full value of life' wrongful death damages in such cases. Also: The plaintiffs argued the defendants waived the right to assert the statutory damages cap by failing to raise it in the pretrial order. The court held the trial court did not abuse its discretion in allowing the defendants to raise the cap for the first time in their post-trial motions, reasoning that the cap statute is not an affirmative defense but a statutory limit on the amount of recoverable damages that is triggered only once a verdict exceeds the threshold. Why it matters: It clarifies that a statutory damages cap need not be raised in the pretrial order or at trial and may be asserted for the first time in a timely post-trial motion. item.title: Crook v. Six Flags Over Georgia II, L.P. (Ga. Ct. App.)
item.description: Plaintiff, the surviving spouse and administrator of an employee who died after falling from a cargo van at a theme park, sued the employer and a co-worker, and the trial court dismissed under OCGA 9-11-12(b)(1) for lack of subject matter jurisdiction based on the exclusive remedy provision of the Workers' Compensation Act. The Court of Appeals held that the Act's exclusivity bar is a statutory affirmative defense, not a question of subject matter jurisdiction, so the employer bears the burden of proving the bar applies and the defense can be waived if not timely raised. The court disapproved Kellogg Co. v. Pinkston, Savannah Hospitality Servs. v. Scriven, and T & R S. Sanitation v. Lowe to the extent they treated the exclusivity bar as jurisdictional. The trial court therefore erred in placing the burden on plaintiff to disprove the bar. item.title: Ya Mon Expeditions, LLC v. YATCO, LLC (11th Cir.)
item.category: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
item.description: In an interlocutory appeal from the denial of a motion to compel arbitration under the FAA, an MLS company sought to compel nonsignatory yacht-seller plaintiffs to arbitrate antitrust claims based on a subscription agreement their brokers allegedly accepted. The court held that under Florida law, which governs the threshold question of whether an arbitration agreement exists, the party seeking to compel arbitration bears the burden of proving an enforceable agreement, and the movant relied on speculation and assumption rather than evidence that the brokers actually listed the plaintiffs' yachts on its website or accepted the relevant version of the agreement. The court rejected the movant's argument that the nonsignatory plaintiffs opposing arbitration bore the burden of disproving its evidence. Why it matters: It clarifies that the FAA presumption favoring arbitration does not apply to the threshold question of whether an agreement to arbitrate exists, and that state law places the burden of proving an enforceable arbitration agreement on the party seeking to compel it. Also: The court held that the nonsignatory plaintiffs could not be bound to arbitrate under an agency-ratification theory. Applying the Florida Supreme Court's full-knowledge requirement, the court held that a principal ratifies an agent's pre-agency acceptance of a contract only on a showing that the principal had full knowledge of the agreement and its terms, and constructive knowledge does not suffice. Because the movant submitted no evidence that the plaintiffs knew of the agreement or its terms, and the brokers' knowledge could not be imputed because it was acquired before any agency relationship formed, ratification did not apply. Why it matters: It establishes that under controlling Florida Supreme Court precedent a nonsignatory principal cannot ratify an agent's pre-agency acceptance of an arbitration agreement absent full actual knowledge of the agreement and its terms. Also: The court held that equitable estoppel did not bind the nonsignatory plaintiffs to arbitrate. A signatory may enforce an arbitration clause against a nonsignatory under equitable estoppel only if the nonsignatory relies on the agreement to assert its claims and the dispute falls within the clause. Because the plaintiffs' federal antitrust claims arose from statutory duties unrelated to the subscription agreement and did not require reference to or construction of that agreement, the plaintiffs were not claiming the benefits of the contract while avoiding its burdens. Why it matters: It clarifies that equitable estoppel cannot compel a nonsignatory to arbitrate where the asserted claims rest on independent statutory duties and do not depend on the contract containing the arbitration clause.
